questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
questions.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}} ${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$
${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$ {{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t)={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t)={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of determinants.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

$$
det(Φ(t))\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by the properties of determinants.

5.Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix?

Consider the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant 2×2 matrix. Let Φ(t) be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that Φ(t) is invertible for all t is given below.

L1: Let x1(t) and x2(t) be the columns of Φ(t)

L2: x1(t) and x2(t) are linearly independent for all t

L3: det(Φ(t))≠0 for all t

L4: Φ(t) is invertible for all t
